ideas.title: Salience-targeted versus anti-targeted vocabulary-column dropout at matched drop rate: a direct test of H1
ideas.description: Here XGBoost's per-tree column subsampling becomes per-batch vocabulary-column dropout in a bag-of-embeddings classifier. For each minibatch, a random subset of vocabulary ids is zeroed in every document of the batch. This differs from i.i.d. per-token word dropout, where each token occurrence is dropped independently. The mechanism test compares three ways of choosing which columns to drop, all at the same expected fraction of dropped token occurrences: (a) uniform, (b) salience-targeted, with drop probability proportional to each token's training-set class-conditional max-PMI, so topic-specific tokens are dropped most often, and (c) anti-targeted, with low-salience tokens dropped most often. If H1 holds, the benefit comes from denying the model its few topic-defining tokens. Then (b) should be at least as good as (a), and (a) should beat (c). If word dropout is generic noise, all three arms should tie. A probe measures reliance concentration directly: the error increase when the top-k PMI tokens of each validation document are masked at test time.
ideas.gap: Open gap 4 asks how explicit regularizers interact with model capacity in small bag-of-words MLPs, and no reviewed paper tests why input-level subsampling helps text bag-of-words models. This idea attacks the regularizer-mechanism half of that gap, together with the transfer of [arXiv:1603.02754]'s column subsampling to a neural bag-of-words model. It uses per-arm tuning (P2) as recommended by [arXiv:2611.14508v1].

ideas.title: Row-wise L1 shrinkage on embeddings vs frequency-matched hard vocabulary pruning: is embedding sparsity a learned regularizer or just vocabulary truncation?
ideas.description: XGBoost's L1 leaf-weight shrinkage [arXiv:1603.02754] transfers to a neural bag-of-embeddings model as a row-wise L1 or group penalty on embedding rows, which is group lasso and therefore known. Applied with a proximal step after each optimizer update, it zeroes whole word rows. The proposed mechanism is that most rows belonging to rare words are pure random-init noise. The model overfits them on 10k labels, and shrinkage removes them. A cheaper confound could explain any gain: frequency-based vocabulary truncation. The proximal penalty may simply zero the rare rows, matching a min-count cut. Each tuned group-lasso run zeroes some set of rows. The decisive control is a hard frequency pruning arm that drops exactly as many of the rarest tokens, plus a random pruning arm that drops the same number of rows at random. If group lasso beats frequency-matched pruning, it is selecting rows by label relevance rather than frequency. This is checked further with an overlap analysis between the zeroed set and the rare-token set, and a frequency-stratified error breakdown. Group lasso is also compared against uniform word dropout (column subsampling) and against the baseline's hidden dropout plus weight decay, all P2-tuned. Each is reported at final and best epoch, together with a tuned cosine-decay schedule arm, to check whether the gains are early stopping in disguise (H2).

Its gain over the hidden-dropout plus weight-decay baseline should persist under best-epoch scoring and against the tuned cosine-decay arm. If group lasso is within 2 SE of frequency-matched pruning, the mechanism is vocabulary truncation (a clean negative).

papers.title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training
papers.summary: Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.

papers.title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology
papers.summary: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner's curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of alpha'beta' cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly's wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there.

ideas.title: Proximal L1 row shrinkage of embeddings versus a frequency-matched vocabulary-pruning control
ideas.description: This idea transfers XGBoost's L1 (alpha) shrinkage to the embedding table as a row-wise group-lasso proximal step after each optimizer update. The step zeroes the entire embedding of any token whose evidence does not justify its cost. A row-lasso gain could come from two different sources. It might be learned, label-aware feature selection, which removes noisy rare tokens. Or it might just be a smaller vocabulary, which removes tokens regardless of label. To separate these, a control arm keeps exactly as many tokens as the shrinkage arm keeps, chosen by a label-blind document-frequency cutoff, and trains them with weight decay. A third arm keeps the same number of tokens chosen by label-aware chi-squared selection. Each arm is ablated against the hidden-dropout plus weight-decay baseline.
ideas.gap: Open gap 2 asks how XGBoost's L1/L2 and subsampling regularizers compare with dropout and weight decay at 10k labels, with comparisons run under P2 tuning per gap 1. This idea attacks that gap by transferring the regularizer into the neural model, instead of benchmarking trees.

hypothesis.claim: Row-wise proximal L1 shrinkage lowers val_top1_err relative to the tuned dropout plus weight-decay baseline. It does so because it performs label-aware vocabulary selection. A label-blind frequency cutoff at the same retained-vocabulary size recovers less than half of the gain. A chi-squared selection at the same size recovers most of it.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: Row-lasso error is at least 1.0 point below the tuned baseline (5 seeds). The frequency-matched pruning arm closes less than 50% of that gap, and the chi-squared arm closes more than 70%. The alternative outcome would also be informative: if the frequency arm matches row-lasso, the gain is mere vocabulary reduction.

ideas.experiment_plan: Edit the regularization code (a proximal row soft-threshold on the embedding table after each step, with threshold lr × λ) and the optimizer step. Use the same proximal step under an SGD-momentum variant if needed for correctness under Adam, and report both. Arms: (0) the tuned baseline, hidden dropout plus weight decay. (1) Row-lasso, λ ∈ {1e-5, 3e-5, 1e-4, 3e-4}, crossed with lr ∈ {0.001, 0.003, 0.01}, 12 trials. (2) Frequency cutoff at the vocabulary size retained by arm 1's best run, plus weight decay, with lr and weight decay tuned over 12 trials. (3) Chi-squared top-K at the same size, plus weight decay, 12 trials. (4) Row-lasso plus hidden dropout combined, 12 trials, to test whether the two stack or substitute. Keep embed_dim, hidden, depth and epochs at their defaults. Rerun each arm's best configuration with 5 seeds. Report the final-epoch and best-epoch error, the peak epoch, the retained vocabulary size, and the frequency histogram of retained tokens. Total is about 85 runs.
ideas.novelty_rationale: Group lasso on embeddings and chi-squared feature selection are both known techniques, and neither is claimed as new. The contribution is the size-matched decomposition into label-aware selection versus vocabulary reduction for a bag-of-embeddings model under per-arm tuning. We did not see this in the reviewed papers, which study tree regularizers on tabular data [arXiv:1603.02754]. That absence does not establish that the decomposition is new, so novelty queries are listed.

design.mechanism: Proximal row shrinkage zeroes the embeddings of tokens whose gradient signal stays below the threshold. These are mostly rare or label-uninformative tokens that otherwise absorb noise in 10k-label training.
design.intervention: A row-wise soft-threshold proximal step on the embedding table, compared with size-matched label-blind (frequency) pruning and label-aware (chi-squared) pruning.
assumptions: Leaf-weight L1 in boosting and row-L1 on randomly initialized embeddings both act as evidence-thresholded feature selection. This holds because both penalize parameters tied to individual sparse input features.
The proximal step remains a meaningful sparsifier when combined with Adam's adaptive update.
design.minimal_test: Run row-lasso at λ=1e-4 and the frequency-matched arm, 3 seeds each, and confirm that row-lasso actually zeroes at least 30% of rows. If it does not, widen the λ grid before running the full study.
design.kill_criterion: Two outcomes end this line. If row-lasso fails to beat the tuned baseline by more than 0.4 points over 5 seeds, the mechanism is reported as a negative result. If the frequency-matched arm is within 0.3 points of row-lasso, the selection mechanism is rejected in favour of plain vocabulary reduction.
confound_controls: The retained-vocabulary size is matched across the pruning arms.
Each arm gets an equal P2 tuning budget.
Best-epoch and peak-epoch reporting addresses H2.
Adam and SGD proximal variants are both reported, so the result is not specific to one optimizer.
design.resource_risk: Low compute, about 85 runs. The risk is that sparsification fails under Adam, which the minimal test checks first.

ideas.title: XGBoost-style column subsampling and L1 shrinkage transferred to neural BoW
ideas.description: XGBoost regularizes sparse inputs with per-tree column subsampling, L1/L2 penalties on leaf weights, and shrinkage. This idea transfers each mechanism to the BoW MLP. Column subsampling becomes word-level input dropout: random vocabulary columns are zeroed per batch, with a fresh vocabulary mask per step. Leaf L1 becomes an L1 penalty on embedding rows, which sparsifies the word features. Shrinkage becomes a low-lr, many-epoch schedule with Polyak/EMA weight averaging.
ideas.gap: Gap 2 (boosting regularizers vs dropout and weight decay on 10k-label text)

hypothesis.claim: Vocabulary-column dropout plus row-wise L1 on the embedding lowers error more than standard hidden dropout plus L2. Most of the gain comes from column subsampling.
hypothesis.predicted_effect: Column subsampling at rate 0.2-0.4 with group-L1 at 1e-6 to 1e-5 gives val_top1_err of about 12.0-12.6, versus 13.3 for the baseline and about 12.8 for tuned hidden dropout plus L2 alone.

ideas.experiment_plan: Augmentation edit: a per-batch mask that drops a fraction p in {0.1, 0.2, 0.4} of vocabulary columns before the embedding sum. Regularization edit: group-L1 (sum of L2 norms of embedding rows) with coefficient in {0, 1e-6, 1e-5, 1e-4}. Schedule edit: lr 1e-3 with EMA decay 0.999 for 16 epochs, versus the default. Ablate each component separately, then combine. Compare against hidden dropout plus weight decay tuned with the same 12-trial budget. Use 3 seeds.
ideas.novelty_rationale: XGBoost reports no text benchmarks, and the review identifies no work that ports its specific regularizers into a neural BoW model as an ablatable set.

papers.summary: This introduction to R is derived from an original set of notes describing the S and S-Plus environments written in 1990-2 by Bill Venables and David M

papers.title: Faster R-CNN: Towards Real-Time Object Detection with Region Proposal Networks
papers.summary: State-of-the-art object detection networks depend on region proposal algorithms to hypothesize object locations. Advances like SPPnet [1] and Fast R-CNN [2] have reduced the running time of these detection networks, exposing region proposal computation as a bottleneck. In this work, we introduce a Region Proposal Network (RPN) that shares full-image convolutional features with the detection network, thus enabling nearly cost-free region proposals. An RPN is a fully convolutional network that simultaneously predicts object bounds and objectness scores at each position. The RPN is trained end-to-end to generate high-quality region proposals, which are used by Fast R-CNN for detection. We further merge RPN and Fast R-CNN into a single network by sharing their convolutional features-using the recently popular terminology of neural networks with 'attention' mechanisms, the RPN component tells the unified network where to look. For the very deep VGG-16 model [3] , our detection system has a frame rate of 5 fps (including all steps) on a GPU, while achieving state-of-the-art object detection accuracy on PASCAL VOC 2007, 2012, and MS COCO datasets with only 300 proposals per image. In ILSVRC and COCO 2015 competitions, Faster R-CNN and RPN are the foundations of the 1st-place winning entries in several tracks. Code has been made publicly available.

papers.title: XGBoost: A Scalable Tree Boosting System
papers.summary: Tree boosting is a highly effective and widely used machine learning method. In this paper, we describe a scalable end-to-end tree boosting system called XGBoost, which is used widely by data scientists to achieve state-of-the-art results on many machine learning challenges. We propose a novel sparsity-aware algorithm for sparse data and weighted quantile sketch for approximate tree learning. More importantly, we provide insights on cache access patterns, data compression and sharding to build a scalable tree boosting system. By combining these insights, XGBoost scales beyond billions of examples using far fewer resources than existing systems.

papers.title: Gradient-based learning applied to document recognition
papers.summary: Multilayer neural networks trained with the back-propagation algorithm constitute the best example of a successful gradient based learning technique. Given an appropriate network architecture, gradient-based learning algorithms can be used to synthesize a complex decision surface that can classify high-dimensional patterns, such as handwritten characters, with minimal preprocessing. This paper reviews various methods applied to handwritten character recognition and compares them on a standard handwritten digit recognition task. Convolutional neural networks, which are specifically designed to deal with the variability of 2D shapes, are shown to outperform all other techniques. Real-life document recognition systems are composed of multiple modules including field extraction, segmentation recognition, and language modeling. A new learning paradigm, called graph transformer networks (GTN), allows such multimodule systems to be trained globally using gradient-based methods so as to minimize an overall performance measure. Two systems for online handwriting recognition are described. Experiments demonstrate the advantage of global training, and the flexibility of graph transformer networks. A graph transformer network for reading a bank cheque is also described. It uses convolutional neural network character recognizers combined with global training techniques to provide record accuracy on business and personal cheques. It is deployed commercially and reads several million cheques per day.

papers.title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale
papers.summary: While the Transformer architecture has become the de-facto standard for natural language processing tasks, its applications to computer vision remain limited. In vision, attention is either applied in conjunction with convolutional networks, or used to replace certain components of convolutional networks while keeping their overall structure in place. We show that this reliance on CNNs is not necessary and a pure transformer applied directly to sequences of image patches can perform very well on image classification tasks. When pre-trained on large amounts of data and transferred to multiple mid-sized or small image recognition benchmarks (ImageNet, CIFAR-100, VTAB, etc.), Vision Transformer (ViT) attains excellent results compared to state-of-the-art convolutional networks while requiring substantially fewer computational resources to train.

papers.title: Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold
papers.summary: Abstract Proteins are essential to life, and understanding their structure can facilitate a mechanistic understanding of their function. Through an enormous experimental effort 1–4 , the structures of around 100,000 unique proteins have been determined 5 , but this represents a small fraction of the billions of known protein sequences 6,7 . Structural coverage is bottlenecked by the months to years of painstaking effort required to determine a single protein structure. Accurate computational approaches are needed to address this gap and to enable large-scale structural bioinformatics. Predicting the three-dimensional structure that a protein will adopt based solely on its amino acid sequence—the structure prediction component of the ‘protein folding problem’ 8 —has been an important open research problem for more than 50 years 9 . Despite recent progress 10–14 , existing methods fall far short of atomic accuracy, especially when no homologous structure is available. Here we provide the first computational method that can regularly predict protein structures with atomic accuracy even in cases in which no similar structure is known. We validated an entirely redesigned version of our neural network-based model, AlphaFold, in the challenging 14th Critical Assessment of protein Structure Prediction (CASP14) 15 , demonstrating accuracy competitive with experimental structures in a majority of cases and greatly outperforming other methods. Underpinning the latest version of AlphaFold is a novel machine learning approach that incorporates physical and biological knowledge about protein structure, leveraging multi-sequence alignments, into the design of the deep learning algorithm.

papers.title: Swin Transformer: Hierarchical Vision Transformer using Shifted Windows
papers.summary: This paper presents a new vision Transformer, called Swin Transformer, that capably serves as a general-purpose backbone for computer vision. Challenges in adapting Transformer from language to vision arise from differences between the two domains, such as large variations in the scale of visual entities and the high resolution of pixels in images compared to words in text. To address these differences, we propose a hierarchical Transformer whose representation is computed with Shifted windows. The shifted windowing scheme brings greater efficiency by limiting self-attention computation to non-overlapping local windows while also allowing for cross-window connection. This hierarchical architecture has the flexibility to model at various scales and has linear computational complexity with respect to image size. These qualities of Swin Transformer make it compatible with a broad range of vision tasks, including image classification (87.3 top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1K) and dense prediction tasks such as object detection (58.7 box AP and 51.1 mask AP on COCO test-dev) and semantic segmentation (53.5 mIoU on ADE20K val). Its performance surpasses the previous state-of-the-art by a large margin of +2.7 box AP and +2.6 mask AP on COCO, and +3.2 mIoU on ADE20K, demonstrating the potential of Transformer-based models as vision backbones. The hierarchical design and the shifted window approach also prove beneficial for all-MLP architectures. The code and models are publicly available at https://github.com/microsoft/Swin-Transformer.

papers.title: GPT-4 Technical Report
papers.summary: We report the development of GPT-4, a large-scale, multimodal model which can accept image and text inputs and produce text outputs. While less capable than humans in many real-world scenarios, GPT-4 exhibits human-level performance on various professional and academic benchmarks, including passing a simulated bar exam with a score around the top 10% of test takers. GPT-4 is a Transformer-based model pre-trained to predict the next token in a document. The post-training alignment process results in improved performance on measures of factuality and adherence to desired behavior. A core component of this project was developing infrastructure and optimization methods that behave predictably across a wide range of scales. This allowed us to accurately predict some aspects of GPT-4's performance based on models trained with no more than 1/1,000th the compute of GPT-4.

papers.title: Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks
papers.summary: We present a scalable approach for semi-supervised learning on graph-structured data that is based on an efficient variant of convolutional neural networks which operate directly on graphs. We motivate the choice of our convolutional architecture via a localized first-order approximation of spectral graph convolutions. Our model scales linearly in the number of graph edges and learns hidden layer representations that encode both local graph structure and features of nodes. In a number of experiments on citation networks and on a knowledge graph dataset we demonstrate that our approach outperforms related methods by a significant margin.

papers.title: Rich Feature Hierarchies for Accurate Object Detection and Semantic Segmentation
papers.summary: Object detection performance, as measured on the canonical PASCAL VOC dataset, has plateaued in the last few years. The best-performing methods are complex ensemble systems that typically combine multiple low-level image features with high-level context. In this paper, we propose a simple and scalable detection algorithm that improves mean average precision (mAP) by more than 30% relative to the previous best result on VOC 2012 -- achieving a mAP of 53.3%. Our approach combines two key insights: (1) one can apply high-capacity convolutional neural networks (CNNs) to bottom-up region proposals in order to localize and segment objects and (2) when labeled training data is scarce, supervised pre-training for an auxiliary task, followed by domain-specific fine-tuning, yields a significant performance boost. Since we combine region proposals with CNNs, we call our method R-CNN: Regions with CNN features. We also present experiments that provide insight into what the network learns, revealing a rich hierarchy of image features. Source code for the complete system is available at http://www.cs.berkeley.edu/~rbg/rcnn.

papers.title: Language Models are Few-Shot Learners
papers.summary: Recent work has demonstrated substantial gains on many NLP tasks and benchmarks by pre-training on a large corpus of text followed by fine-tuning on a specific task. While typically task-agnostic in architecture, this method still requires task-specific fine-tuning datasets of thousands or tens of thousands of examples. By contrast, humans can generally perform a new language task from only a few examples or from simple instructions - something which current NLP systems still largely struggle to do. Here we show that scaling up language models greatly improves task-agnostic, few-shot performance, sometimes even reaching competitiveness with prior state-of-the-art fine-tuning approaches. Specifically, we train GPT-3, an autoregressive language model with 175 billion parameters, 10x more than any previous non-sparse language model, and test its performance in the few-shot setting. For all tasks, GPT-3 is applied without any gradient updates or fine-tuning, with tasks and few-shot demonstrations specified purely via text interaction with the model. GPT-3 achieves strong performance on many NLP datasets, including translation, question-answering, and cloze tasks, as well as several tasks that require on-the-fly reasoning or domain adaptation, such as unscrambling words, using a novel word in a sentence, or performing 3-digit arithmetic. At the same time, we also identify some datasets where GPT-3's few-shot learning still struggles, as well as some datasets where GPT-3 faces methodological issues related to training on large web corpora. Finally, we find that GPT-3 can generate samples of news articles which human evaluators have difficulty distinguishing from articles written by humans. We discuss broader societal impacts of this finding and of GPT-3 in general.

papers.title: MobileNets: Efficient Convolutional Neural Networks for Mobile Vision Applications
papers.summary: We present a class of efficient models called MobileNets for mobile and embedded vision applications. MobileNets are based on a streamlined architecture that uses depth-wise separable convolutions to build light weight deep neural networks. We introduce two simple global hyper-parameters that efficiently trade off between latency and accuracy. These hyper-parameters allow the model builder to choose the right sized model for their application based on the constraints of the problem. We present extensive experiments on resource and accuracy tradeoffs and show strong performance compared to other popular models on ImageNet classification. We then demonstrate the effectiveness of MobileNets across a wide range of applications and use cases including object detection, finegrain classification, face attributes and large scale geo-localization.

papers.title: The Llama 3 Herd of Models
papers.summary: Modern artificial intelligence (AI) systems are powered by foundation models. This paper presents a new set of foundation models, called Llama 3. It is a herd of language models that natively support multilinguality, coding, reasoning, and tool usage. Our largest model is a dense Transformer with 405B parameters and a context window of up to 128K tokens. This paper presents an extensive empirical evaluation of Llama 3. We find that Llama 3 delivers comparable quality to leading language models such as GPT-4 on a plethora of tasks. We publicly release Llama 3, including pre-trained and post-trained versions of the 405B parameter language model and our Llama Guard 3 model for input and output safety. The paper also presents the results of experiments in which we integrate image, video, and speech capabilities into Llama 3 via a compositional approach. We observe this approach performs competitively with the state-of-the-art on image, video, and speech recognition tasks. The resulting models are not yet being broadly released as they are still under development.

papers.title: LLaMA: Open and Efficient Foundation Language Models
papers.summary: We introduce LLaMA, a collection of foundation language models ranging from 7B to 65B parameters. We train our models on trillions of tokens, and show that it is possible to train state-of-the-art models using publicly available datasets exclusively, without resorting to proprietary and inaccessible datasets. In particular, LLaMA-13B outperforms GPT-3 (175B) on most benchmarks, and LLaMA-65B is competitive with the best models, Chinchilla-70B and PaLM-540B. We release all our models to the research community.

papers.title: Medical Image Segmentation: Foundation Model Adaptation versus Task-Specific Training
papers.summary: Foundation models pretrained on large natural-image collections are increasingly adapted for medical image segmentation, in the expectation that they will replace models trained for each task. Most comparisons, however, use data from the training distribution and a single task-specific baseline whose configuration is rarely justified, and therefore provide limited evidence of performance at new clinical sites. It also remains unclear how much of a foundation model must be adapted, and what determines this. We adapted a foundation model, DINOv2, with strategies ranging from tuning only its bias terms to full fine-tuning, and compared it with U-Nets and ResU-Nets trained from scratch. Experiments covered colonoscopy, breast ultrasound and dermoscopy, with testing on held-out data from the training source and on independent datasets from other institutions. The adapted foundation model generalised better on every external dataset. Within the training distribution, the task-specific models remained competitive when training data were abundant, and delineated boundaries more precisely, while the foundation model more often missed small lesions. Only a small fraction of the foundation model required adaptation, and the capacity needed was determined by the imaging domain rather than by the adaptation method. A widely used polyp test set was also found to duplicate images from another benchmark. Foundation-model adaptation is therefore warranted where models must work across sites, with capacity selected on the target domain.

papers.title: Toward Foundation Detection Models via Example-Based Grounding in EM-DETR
papers.summary: DeepLearning (DL)-based Computer-Aided Diagnostic (CAD) systems have shown great promise in supporting clinicians, but their performance heavily depends on the availability of large, well-annotated datasets. In medical lesion detection, the scarcity of comprehensive, stan dardized annotations and the heterogeneity of existing datasets limit the development of robust foundation models. In this work, we introduce a novel approach to building a multi-domain foundation model for le sion detection by integrating diverse medical image datasets annotated for both anatomical structures and abnormalities. We first propose a student-teacher training strategy to effectively combine datasets with heterogeneous label spaces, mitigating catastrophic forgetting, and im proving feature learning. In addition, building on our previously pro posed example-based EM-DETR framework, we adapt it to jointly learn from multiple domain-specific datasets, enabling fine-grained, example driven detection across modalities. Our model achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) results, with image-level AUC scores exceeding previous SOTA by 1% point on four key findings in CXRs. We achieve a leading mAP50 in CXRs and mammography, surpassing EM-DETR trained on a single dataset by 2-3% points. This approach paves the way for scalable foundation models in medical imaging that leverage heterogeneous data while maintaining robust and generalizable performance.

papers.title: Contrastive Discovery: Open-Ended Scientific Discovery over Competing Explanations
papers.summary: LLM agents are increasingly used for open-ended, data-driven scientific discovery, yet most of them evaluate hypotheses pointwise, testing an empirical claim $h$ only against its complement $\neg h$. When evidence rejects $h$, the agent learns that one explanation is unlikely but not which alternative the evidence supports. To recover that alternative, we introduce Contrastive Discovery, which replaces the single hypothesis with a contrast set, a scientific question paired with mutually exclusive and collectively exhaustive competing explanations. Each experiment is scored by how its evidence redistributes belief across the set, and the question is resolved when belief concentrates on one explanation. Because contrast sets change only the unit an agent proposes and scores, an existing agent can use them to re-evaluate evidence it has already collected or to guide its search. Across six domains, $89\%$ of the pointwise candidates with the largest belief shifts are rejections. On the same evidence, contrast sets resolve $73\%$ of these candidates to a specific alternative. When contrast sets guide search, the agent resolves $67\%$ more questions than pointwise surprisal under the same experiment budget. In a blinded study, $38$ human experts chose the same explanation on $78\%$ of resolved questions and on $82\%$ of questions where the pointwise agent rejected its hypothesis and stopped. Together, these results support explicit competing explanations as a way for discovery agents to resolve more scientific questions from the same evidence and validation budget.

papers.title: Online Graph Coloring: Competitive Ratios Separating Randomized and Deterministic Algorithms
papers.summary: We study online coloring, focusing on the competitive ratio. The best previously known results were (1) a lower bound of $Ω(n / \log^2 n)$ for both deterministic and randomized algorithms by Halldórsson and Szegedy (1994), (2) an upper bound of $O(n / \log n)$ for randomized algorithms by Halldórsson (1997), and (3) an upper bound of $O(n / \log \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms by Kawarabayashi, Yoneda, and Yoneda (2025). In this paper, we improve these results as follows: 1. A new lower bound of $Ω(n / \log n)$ for deterministic algorithms. 2. A new upper bound of $O(n (\log \log n)^2 / \log^2 n)$ for randomized algorithms. 3. A new upper bound of $O(n / (\log \log n)^{2-\varepsilon})$ for deterministic algorithms for every fixed $\varepsilon>0$. For randomized algorithms, we nearly close the gap between the lower and upper bounds; the remaining gap is only $O((\log \log n)^2)$. We establish the asymptotic separation between randomized and deterministic online graph coloring. Against an oblivious adversary, a polynomial-time randomized algorithm achieves a competitive ratio asymptotically smaller than any deterministic algorithm can guarantee, even with unlimited computation.

papers.title: Pyrite: Building and Benchmarking Protein-Ligand Pose Ranking Agents
papers.summary: Predicting how a ligand binds to its target is central to small-molecule drug discovery. Modern cofolding models can generate diverse candidate poses, but reliably ranking these candidates remains challenging. We introduce Pyrite, a pairwise pose-ranking benchmark comprising 1,500 pose pairs across diverse protein-ligand complexes. Expert chemists equipped with 3D visualization tools and physics-based scores perform near chance, highlighting the difficulty of interpreting available chemical signals. To investigate automated ranking, we introduce PyriteRep, a structured representation of molecular geometry, protein-ligand interactions, and physicochemical scores, and develop two LLM-based agents: PyriteReasoner, which directly compares poses through text-based reasoning, and PyriteFeaturizer, which generates executable code to construct features for logistic regression, optionally incorporating features derived from LLM subcalls. These agents achieve up to 67% and 74% accuracy, respectively, exceeding observed expert performance. LLM-guided feature discovery generally outperforms direct reasoning, while Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) improves open-weight models, enabling them to match or surpass closed-source frontier models in our evaluations. These results establish Pyrite as a challenging test of pose-ranking ability and highlight LLM-guided feature discovery as a promising approach to interpret and combine the outputs of computational chemistry tools.

papers.title: When Does the Real Wiring Win? Testing connectome structure-function claims against unmeasured physiology
papers.summary: Connectome-constrained models are often used to argue that a measured wiring diagram outperforms shuffled or rewired wiring, and hence that structure shapes function. Such comparisons can confound wiring with how the models are tuned: a connectome fixes who connects to whom, not the excitability, gains or plasticity rates the model also needs, and modellers often tune these until the real-wiring model works. We separate three estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 restricted to physiology consistent with independent data (P3). The biases involved are known in machine learning (under-tuned baselines, inherited weights, winner's curse); we measure what they do to biological conclusions, using synthetic ground truth, placebo nulls and three Drosophila circuit models. Some claims survive every protocol we test: segregated reward and punishment dopamine improves learning, and head-direction topography is required for a persistent bump. Others do not. In the mushroom body, the real Kenyon-cell output wiring beats a cross-subtype identity shuffle by 0.09 under P1 and P2 but loses to it by 0.09 under P3 (95% CIs exclude zero; held-out runs confirm). The verdict is set by the share of alpha'beta' cells among active Kenyon cells, which P1 selects low; at the share implied by imaging (about 44%) the real-wiring model fails to learn, exposing a model inadequacy rather than a deficit of the fly's wiring. In flyvis, P1 penalises a mirrored connectome, which has a constructed solution within 0.07 (median) of the real error, more than a spatially shuffled one in 50 of 50 members; the ranking survives ten-fold longer retraining but depends on the checkpoint at fifty-fold. A credible structural claim needs matched optimisation, data-constrained physiology and a model that still works there.

review_snapshot.overview: The supplied list is almost entirely off-topic for regularization of small bag-of-words text classifiers on a 10k AG News subset. None of the papers studies dropout, weight decay, label smoothing, early stopping, data augmentation, or similar regularizers for text classification under limited labels. Most entries are highly cited landmarks from other areas: vision detection and backbones, protein structure, foundation LLMs, and graph SSL. There are also 2026 preprints on unrelated subjects such as graph coloring, connectomes, and pose ranking. A few are only indirectly relevant: [arXiv:1603.02754] gives a strong regularized, sparsity-aware baseline for BoW features; [arXiv:1609.02907] offers a semi-supervised route for limited labels; [arXiv:2005.14165] is a few-shot alternative to training small models. Methodological cautions in [arXiv:2611.14508v1] and [arXiv:2611.14519v1] about under-tuned baselines are directly applicable to how regularization comparisons should be run. The colleague should treat this list as a weak evidence base. The gaps below are experiments the setting can answer, not conclusions the papers support.

themes.name: Strong non-neural baselines for sparse BoW features
themes.summary: Gradient-boosted trees with explicit L1/L2 penalties, shrinkage and column subsampling, plus sparsity-aware split finding, are a natural, heavily regularized competitor to small neural BoW classifiers. The paper benchmarks mostly tabular tasks, not text.

themes.name: Learning from limited labels via structure or pretraining
themes.summary: Two routes are represented. Graph-based semi-supervised propagation [arXiv:1609.02907] leverages unlabelled neighbours. Large-scale pretraining, then transfer or few-shot use, appears in [arXiv:2005.14165], [arXiv:1311.2524], [arXiv:2010.11929], [arXiv:2302.13971], [arXiv:2407.21783] and [arXiv:2303.08774]. These treat pretraining as the main regularizer when labels are scarce, but none isolates it against classic regularizers for small models.

themes.name: Fair comparison and tuning-budget methodology
themes.summary: These papers warn that comparisons are biased when baselines are under-tuned or inherit hyperparameters tuned on the favoured model [arXiv:2611.14508v1]. [arXiv:2611.14519v1] makes the same point about single, unjustified task-specific baselines and about how much of a model to adapt (from bias-only tuning to full fine-tuning). Both apply directly to regularization ablations.

themes.name: Architecture and capacity control
themes.summary: Capacity reduction through architecture is a form of implicit regularization. Examples are width multipliers [arXiv:1704.04861] and convolutional weight sharing [doi:10.1109/5.726791]. All evidence is from vision.

themes.name: Off-topic entries
themes.summary: These papers have no bearing on text classifier regularization.

paper_notes.contribution: Regularized boosting objective (L1/L2 on leaf weights, shrinkage, subsampling) with sparsity-aware splits suited to high-dimensional sparse inputs like BoW.
paper_notes.limitation: No text-classification or low-label experiments; whether it beats a tuned linear or MLP BoW model on 10k AG News is untested here.

paper_notes.contribution: Semi-supervised node classification by propagating features over a graph, effective with very few labels.
paper_notes.limitation: It requires a graph, such as a document kNN or word co-occurrence graph, which AG News does not provide. Results are on citation networks, not news topics.

paper_notes.contribution: Shows scale enables few-shot classification without gradient updates, an alternative to training regularized small models.
paper_notes.limitation: Compute cost is incomparable to a small BoW model. It gives no evidence about what regularizes small models trained from scratch.

paper_notes.contribution: Formalizes three tuning estimands: physiology tuned on the real wiring and transferred to nulls (P1), each wiring tuned on its own (P2), and P2 constrained by independent data (P3). It shows how tuning on the favoured model biases comparisons.
paper_notes.limitation: Its domain is neuroscience, and it gives no empirical ML regularization results. The transfer to ML ablations is by analogy.

paper_notes.contribution: Compares adaptation depths (bias-only through full fine-tuning) against from-scratch baselines with justified configurations.
paper_notes.limitation: It covers medical segmentation only, not text or BoW.

paper_notes.contribution: Global width and resolution multipliers trade capacity against accuracy.
paper_notes.limitation: The evidence is from vision. Width as a regularizer for small-data text MLPs is not studied.

paper_notes.contribution: Shows architectural priors (weight sharing) reduce effective capacity and improve generalization.
paper_notes.limitation: Its BoW inputs discard word order, so convolutional priors do not carry over directly.

gaps.gap: Does a fully tuned regularized linear model (logistic regression with L2 or L1 on TF-IDF BoW) match or beat a small MLP on val_top1_err on the 10k AG News subset? The test is to give each model its own hyperparameter search with an equal trial budget.
gaps.why_open: No listed paper evaluates this setting. [arXiv:2611.14508v1] and [arXiv:2611.14519v1] show that comparisons under unequal tuning are biased, so any claimed regularization gain needs per-model tuning (the P2 estimand).

gaps.gap: Gradient-boosted trees versus neural BoW classifiers at 10k labels, comparing XGBoost's L1/L2 and subsampling regularizers against dropout and weight decay.
gaps.why_open: [arXiv:1603.02754] claims strength on sparse data but reports no text-classification benchmarks.

gaps.gap: Whether a kNN document graph built over the full AG News training pool, with labels only on the 10k subset, lowers error relative to supervised-only regularization when used for graph propagation.
gaps.why_open: [arXiv:1609.02907] needs a given graph. How much a constructed similarity graph helps over dropout or weight decay alone has not been measured for BoW text.

gaps.gap: Interaction of explicit regularizers (dropout, weight decay, label smoothing, early stopping) with model width in small BoW MLPs. Do they substitute for each other or stack?
gaps.why_open: Width-as-capacity is studied only in vision [arXiv:1704.04861]. No listed paper crosses width with explicit regularizers on text.

gaps.gap: Cost-matched comparison: a frozen pretrained embedding or LLM few-shot baseline versus a from-scratch regularized BoW model at equal labelled data.
gaps.why_open: [arXiv:2005.14165] and [arXiv:2302.13971] imply pretraining dominates, but they never compare against a properly regularized small model under compute or latency constraints.

trends: Pretraining at scale is increasingly treated as the default answer to label scarcity, displacing explicit regularization research ([arXiv:2005.14165], [arXiv:2407.21783]).
Growing scrutiny of baseline tuning and fair comparisons ([arXiv:2611.14508v1], [arXiv:2611.14519v1]).
Partial or parameter-efficient adaptation (for example bias-only tuning) as an implicit regularizer ([arXiv:2611.14519v1]).
The supplied corpus contains almost no direct work on small text-classifier regularization, so the relevant literature must be gathered elsewhere.

steer.interest: I want to know which cheap regularizers actually help a small bag-of-embeddings text classifier when labels are scarce, and why, rather than collecting another leaderboard point.
hunches: Word dropout helps mostly because it stops the model from leaning on a few topic-specific tokens, not because it acts like generic noise.
Part of any reported gain is early stopping in disguise: a regularized model simply peaks later within the same epoch budget.
avoid: Pure hyperparameter sweeps with no mechanism behind them
steer.contribution: A mechanism claim with a matched control; a clean negative result is welcome.
known: A logistic-regression baseline reaches about 13.3% error on this split

direction_map.name: Targeted versus random word dropout
direction_map.thesis: If word dropout works by breaking reliance on a few topic-specific tokens, then dropping only the most class-informative tokens should capture most of the gain. Dropping the same number of uninformative tokens should capture little of it.
direction_map.steer_link: Tests H1 directly. The dropout rate is held fixed, and only which tokens are eligible to be dropped changes. A gain that tracks token informativeness supports H1's 'leaning on a few tokens' story over 'generic noise'.
direction_map.gap: No reviewed paper studies dropout for BoW text (overview). Gap 4 lists dropout among the untested explicit regularizers for small BoW MLPs.
direction_map.open_question: Does the val error reduction from word dropout depend on which tokens are dropped at a matched expected drop count? Does it shrink the share of logit mass carried by the top-k tokens per document?
direction_map.first_experiment: 1. Rank vocabulary by chi-square or mutual information with the label on the training split. 2. Train the default MLP under four conditions: no dropout; uniform word dropout at p=0.1; dropout restricted to the top-5% informative tokens, rate set to match the expected tokens dropped per doc; dropout restricted to the bottom-50% tokens, also count-matched. 3. Use 3 seeds and the 8-epoch budget, giving roughly 12 short runs. 4. Report val_top1_err. 5. Report a concentration statistic: the fraction of the summed |gradient×input| attribution from each doc's top 3 tokens.
direction_map.risk: At 10k docs with an 8-epoch budget, all dropout variants may land within seed noise of each other (±0.3%), and none may beat 13.3. The result would then say nothing about mechanism.

direction_map.name: Is it just later peaking? Best-epoch-matched comparison
direction_map.thesis: Regularizer gains under a fixed 8-epoch budget may disappear once each model is evaluated at its own best epoch with its own tuned learning rate and epoch count. Under this reading, the regularizer only shifts when the model peaks.
direction_map.steer_link: Argues with H2 by stating what would make it wrong. H2 is false if the regularized model's best-epoch error is still lower than the unregularized model's best-epoch error after both get an equal tuning budget over lr and epochs. H2 is true if the gap closes.
direction_map.gap: Gap 1 and the tuning-estimand methodology: comparisons where only one arm is tuned are biased. Here that means comparing against a baseline whose stopping point was not tuned.
direction_map.open_question: After matching per-model tuning of lr and stopping epoch, how much of the dropout, weight-decay or label-smoothing gain remains?
direction_map.first_experiment: 1. Train each arm with per-epoch val logging and epochs extended to 30: baseline (weight decay 1e-4, no dropout), word dropout, and label smoothing 0.1. 2. Give each arm the same 6-point lr grid. 3. Record the oracle best-epoch error and the epoch at which it occurs. 4. Compare the fixed-8-epoch gain with the best-epoch-matched gain. 5. Use 3 seeds.
direction_map.risk: Oracle best-epoch selection on val is optimistically biased for every arm. Small residual gaps (<0.3%) may then be uninterpretable without a held-out split taken from the 10k.

direction_map.name: Token-structured versus matched generic noise
direction_map.thesis: H1 is wrong if structure-free noise reproduces word dropout's gain when matched for perturbation magnitude. Two such controls are Gaussian noise added to the pooled embedding and dropout on embedding dimensions.
direction_map.steer_link: This is the matched control H1 itself implies. H1 claims the gain is 'not because it acts like generic noise', so the test equalizes noise magnitude and checks whether token structure matters at all.
direction_map.gap: Gap 4: there is no evidence on whether explicit regularizers on text substitute for each other. Matching the perturbation magnitude makes it possible to tell the mechanisms apart.
direction_map.open_question: Measured at the pooled representation, does word dropout beat dimension dropout and Gaussian noise when all three induce the same variance?
direction_map.first_experiment: 1. Measure the per-example variance of the pooled embedding under word dropout at p=0.1. 2. Calibrate Gaussian sigma and embedding-dimension dropout rate so each produces the same variance. 3. Train all three arms plus a no-noise arm, using 3 seeds and default knobs. 4. Compare val_top1_err.
direction_map.risk: Variance matching may be too crude, because word dropout also changes the mean through its interaction with document length. Equal results could then reflect miscalibration rather than a real equivalence.

direction_map.name: Width versus explicit regularization: substitutes or stack?
direction_map.thesis: In a bag-of-embeddings MLP, embed_dim and hidden width may act as the dominant regularizer. Once capacity is tuned, explicit regularizers may add nothing, and a properly tuned linear model may remain the one to beat.
direction_map.steer_link: Comes from the literature rather than the hunches. The capacity-control papers and Gap 1 suggest the 13.3 linear baseline may be hard to beat at all. If that holds, the question 'which cheap regularizer helps' reduces to capacity.
direction_map.gap: Gaps 1 and 4: capacity and explicit regularizers have never been crossed for text, and per-model tuning is required.
direction_map.open_question: Across embed_dim in {8, 16, 64, 128}, does the best achievable error with dropout plus weight decay fall below the best achievable error without them?
direction_map.first_experiment: 1. Cross 4 embed_dim values with 2 regularizer settings (none vs word dropout 0.1 + weight decay 1e-3). 2. Hold hidden=embed_dim and depth=1. 3. Give each cell a 3-point lr grid and use 2 seeds. 4. Plot the error-versus-width curves.
direction_map.risk: Every cell may sit at or above 13.3. That clean negative would show small MLPs cannot beat linear BoW here, but it would not identify any mechanism.

direction_map.name: Boosting-style regularizers transferred to a neural bag-of-words...
direction_map.thesis: Boosting-style regularizers transferred to a neural bag-of-words classifier: per-batch vocabulary-column subsampling (word-level input dropout) and L1 shrinkage on embedding rows, each ablated against hidden dropout plus weight decay
